title: Scientific Calculator: Parentheses, Powers, Factorials, Percent
description: Just + − × ÷, parentheses, √, powers, factorials and percent; percent is a suffix ÷100, so 200+10% is 200.1, and output keeps 12 significant digits.
content:
On this site, the online calculator is a page that evaluates an expression right in front of you: it shows the result as you type and only commits when you press = or Enter. It has no sin/cos/log/π and no DEG/RAD angle-mode switch; what it does is the four basic operations, parentheses, √, powers, factorials and percent. The sections below go through precedence, formatting and the edge cases as the real implementation handles them.

1. First, what it is: 24 keys and a result as you type

The keypad has 24 keys: C, ⌫, (, ), n!, √, xʸ, ÷, 7, 8, 9, ×, 4, 5, 6, −, 1, 2, 3, +, ±, 0, . and =. The placeholder of the input field #calcExpr is 0 and its maxlength is 2000; the heading above reads “Current result”, and the output #calcResult below starts at 0.

Every input event recomputes: inside render() the script reads the field value, treats an empty string as 0, and writes the result straight back to the output. Only = or Enter calls calculate(): on success it hides the status bar and writes the result into the “Calculation history” column on the right; only on failure does it show an error message and mark the field aria-invalid. So live typing and committing are two different paths. Both the field and the output carry readable names: the label in front of the field is “Expression”, the output has aria-label “Current result”, and the status bar is a role=status aria-live region for assistive technology.

2. Precedence: postfix binds tightest, powers associate to the right, unary signs wrap a power

The postfix operators ! and % bind tightest and chain from left to right: 3!! is (3!)! = 720, 2^3! is 2^(3!) = 64, and 5!% is 1.2. They act only on the value immediately before them and never wrap the whole expression.

^ associates to the right and parses one complete unary expression on its right: 2^3^2 is 2^(3^2) = 512, 2^-3 is 0.125, and 2^√9 is 2^3 = 8. Only (2^3)^2 gives 64.

Unary +, - and √ wrap the entire unary expression that follows: -2^2 computes 2^2 first and then negates, giving -4; √9^2 computes 9^2 first and then takes the root, giving 9. Note that √(x²) and (√x)² are equal anyway when x ≥ 0, so this example cannot tell the two readings apart; √9! can: it computes √362880 ≈ 602.395219105, while (√9)! is 6.

Below that come * and /, and last + and -, with the same level evaluated left to right: 1-2-3 is -4, not 2, and 8/4/2 is 1, not 4. Mixed expressions follow the levels above; when in doubt, add parentheses. Parentheses change only the order of evaluation, not any of the rules above; too many, too few or an empty pair all raise syntax, and the page never closes brackets for you.

3. Percent is a suffix that divides by 100, not “percent of the number on the left”

Percent is a postfix operator meaning “divide this value by 100”, not “percent of the number on the left”. So 50% is 0.5, 200*10% is 20, and 200+10% is 200.1 — not 220. 1%+1 is 1.01 and 100%-1 is 0.

To say “add 10%” you have to write it out: 200*(1+10%) evaluates 1+0.1 inside the parentheses first and gives 220; 200+200*10% gives 220 as well. For a discount, 200*(1-10%) = 180. Expressions like these depend on the parentheses, so do not treat percent as syntax sugar that automatically tracks the left operand.

4. Factorial takes non-negative integers only, and 170 is a hard ceiling

Factorial accepts non-negative integers only: 5! = 120, 0! = 1, and 3!! chains twice to give 720. 171! fails outright with “The result is too large.” because the code hard-codes the ceiling at 170; 170! is still finite at 7.25741561531e+306. (-3)! and 2.5! fail with “This operation has no real result. Factorials require a non-negative integer.” because factorial needs an integer that is not negative.

Another easy misreading is the order of factorial against power: 2^3! is 2^6 = 64, not (2^3)! = 40320; for the latter you must write the parentheses. Factorials grow very fast: 170! is about 7.26e306, still inside Number.MAX_VALUE, while 171! is about 1.24e309 and already outside it, which is why the code puts the ceiling at 170.

5. Square root, power, and the keys it does not have

√ takes a square root only, with no cube root or n-th root, and xʸ is just ^, with no separate power-function key. The page has no sin, cos, tan, log, ln, π or e keys and no DEG/RAD switch — many “how to use a scientific calculator” tutorials online open with angle mode, but this page has no angle mode, so reach for another tool when you need trigonometry or logarithms. In implementation terms, the tokenizer recognises only digits and the characters + - * / ^ ( ) ! % √; letters never enter the token stream, so sin(30) or π is rejected by the evaluator as syntax, and with no trigonometric functions an angle mode would have nothing to act on.

On the edges: √(-1) and √-4 fail with “This operation has no real result. Factorials require a non-negative integer.” because the result is NaN; 1e308*10 and 9^9^9 fail with “The result is too large.” because they exceed the double-precision ceiling; 1e999 is already read as Infinity at the lexing stage and fails the same way. None of these print Infinity or NaN on the screen.

6. Twelve significant digits: the screen shows a display value, not the exact value

The display value goes through formatArithmetic: keep 12 significant digits first, then hand it to the shortest representation JavaScript produces. So 1/3 shows 0.333333333333, 2/3 shows 0.666666666667 (the last digit rounds up), and 1/7 shows 0.142857142857.

The 12-digit formatting hides floating-point residue: 0.1+0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in double precision but displays as 0.3; amplify the residue and you can see it — 0.1+0.2-0.3 shows 5.55111512313e-17. A screen that reads 0.3 does not mean 0.3 is what is stored.

Large integers are rewritten too, for two different reasons. The double-precision value of 1e15+1 is exactly 1000000000000001, but 12 significant digits only leave room for 1000000000000000, so the lost 1 comes from formatting rather than from floating-point storage; the exact value of 20! is 2432902008176640000 and it displays as 2432902008180000000, a 12-digit rounding; 1234567890123456 displays as 1234567890120000; and 2^53+1 already equals 9007199254740992 in double precision, which is then formatted to 9007199254740000.

Exponent notation follows JavaScript as well: 10^21 shows 1e+21, 1e-7 shows 1e-7, and -0 is normalised to 0. When you read a result, look for an e first, then decide whether it is an integer or an approximation.

7. Five error messages: when one appears and which one

Errors appear in the status bar only on commit — =, Enter and the equals key all count as a commit; while you are typing, the result just becomes “—” and copy is disabled, with no message. The five messages are fixed: syntax “Check the expression and parentheses.”, division “Division by zero is undefined.”, domain “This operation has no real result. Factorials require a non-negative integer.”, range “The result is too large.”, and limit “The expression is too long or too deeply nested.”.

The triggers are: an unbalanced pair, an operator at the end, or an unrecognised character (2&3, 2(3)) → syntax; a zero divisor (1/0, 0/0, 1/(1-1)) → division; √ of a negative number, or factorial of a negative number or a fraction → domain; a non-finite result (1e308*10, 9^9^9, 1e999) → range; more than 2000 characters, more than 1024 tokens, or more than 128 levels of parenthesis nesting → limit.

  • syntax: Check the expression and parentheses. Examples: 2+, (), 2(3).
  • division: Division by zero is undefined. Examples: 1/0, 0/0, 1/(1-1).
  • domain: This operation has no real result. Factorials require a non-negative integer. Examples: √(-1), (-3)!, 2.5!.
  • range: The result is too large. Examples: 171!, 1e308*10, 1e999.
  • limit: The expression is too long or too deeply nested. Examples: 1025 tokens, 2001 characters, 129 levels of parentheses.

8. Calculation history, copy and the keyboard

The “Calculation history” column on the right lives in memory only: every successful = inserts an entry, newest at the top, at most 20 entries, and an entry identical to the latest one (same expression, same result) is not added twice. Selecting a record puts its expression back into the field and recomputes at once; “Clear” is disabled while there are no records; the empty state reads “Your calculations will appear here.” and the note reads “Select a calculation to use it again. Records last only for this visit.”. Refresh or close the page and it is gone, with no localStorage. Each record spans two lines: the expression on top and “= result” below; “Clear” empties only the history and leaves the field and the current result untouched.

“Copy result” copies the current result string, and the button is disabled while the result is “—”. There are two keyboards: with focus in the field, Enter or = calculates and Escape clears; with focus outside the field (on blank page space or in the keypad), digits and + - * / ( ) ! % ^ √ insert directly, Enter/= calculates, Backspace deletes one character and Escape clears. When focus sits in another field, a select or a link, the global shortcuts stay inactive, which keeps them from hijacking typed input.

± flips the sign of a plain numeric literal directly (9 → -9 → 9) and wraps any other expression as a whole, turning 2+3 into -(2+3) = -5. √ wraps the expression as √(…) when the expression is non-empty and the current result is valid, and otherwise just inserts a single √; xʸ does the same, turning 2 into (2)^, after which 3 gives 8. After you press =, a digit, ( or . starts a new expression, + − × ÷ continue from the current result, and √ or xʸ wraps the whole current expression — 2+3, =, then √ gives √(2+3) = 2.2360679775, while xʸ gives (2+3)^.

Two details are worth remembering: an invalid live result shows “—” and disables the copy button at the same time, so a “—” is not a frozen page; history deduplication compares only the latest entry, so pressing = twice in a row does not create two identical records.

9. Putting it into a workflow: neighbouring tools and the limits

A finished value often has to land in a concrete setting: to turn seconds into a date use the timestamp converter, to count the days between two dates use the date difference calculator, and for length, weight or temperature use the unit converter. This calculator itself does no units, exchange rates, dates or statistics and saves nothing; for money, convert the amount to integer cents first so that residues such as 0.1 in double precision do not creep in.

To close, the limits in one place: no trigonometry, logarithms, π/e constants or angle mode; no memory keys (M+/MR); history is not persisted; the expression caps are 2000 characters, 1024 tokens and 128 levels of nesting; and only real numbers are supported — no complex numbers, fractions or arbitrary precision. When you need arbitrary precision or trigonometry, switch to a dedicated tool rather than forcing the calculation here.

faqs.q: Can this calculator do sin, cos or log?
faqs.a: No. The page has no sin, cos, tan, log or ln keys, no π or e constant keys and no DEG/RAD angle-mode switch. It supports only the four basic operations, parentheses, √, ^, !, % and unary plus/minus; for trigonometry or logarithms use a dedicated tool.

Because % is a postfix operator: it first divides the 10 right in front of it by 100 to get 0.1, then evaluates 200+0.1, which gives 200.1. To add 10%, write 200*(1+10%) or 200+200*10%; both give 220.

The addition is exact in double precision — 1000000000000001 — but the display function formatArithmetic keeps only 12 significant digits, and the 1 falls in the 16th place, so it is dropped. With larger numbers precision can be lost before formatting as well: for example 2^53+1 already equals 9007199254740992 in double precision.

Factorial hard-codes its ceiling at 170 in the code: 171! fails with “The result is too large.” 170! still yields a finite value, 7.25741561531e+306, and anything larger leaves the range double precision can represent. A negative or fractional factorial fails with “This operation has no real result. Factorials require a non-negative integer.”.

faqs.q: Does the history survive to my next visit?
faqs.a: No. The history lives in an in-memory array only, so refreshing or closing the page clears it; it keeps at most the 20 most recent entries and skips an entry identical to the latest one (same expression and same result). The page does not use localStorage.

faqs.q: Why does the result show “—” while I type?
faqs.a: “—” means the current expression cannot be evaluated yet, for example when you have typed only 2+ or a parenthesis is unclosed. No message appears during live typing; only after you commit with = or Enter is the matching message shown and the field marked aria-invalid.

focus: The evaluator in this online calculator is a small hand-written bounded grammar, not eval: postfix ! and % bind tightest, ^ associates to the right and eats one unary expression, unary - and √ wrap the whole unary expression that follows, which is why -2^2 gives -4 and √9! equals √362880; % is a postfix divide-by-100 rather than “percent of”; display always goes through 12-significant-digit formatting, which rewrites large integers and floating-point residue; five errors each carry a fixed message, and history is in memory only, capped at 20 entries; the page has no trigonometry, logarithms, π/e or angle mode.
